content: Ryegrass, scientifically classified under the genus Lolium, consists of nine species of tufted grasses belonging to the subfamily Pooideae within the family Poaceae. These grasses exhibit a characteristic bunch-like growth pattern. While they are sometimes referred to as tares, there is no definitive evidence linking them to the plant described by that name in English translations of the Bible, such as in the Parable of the Tares. Other candidates for the biblical tares include vetches. Ryegrass species are native to Europe, Asia, and northern Africa, but they have been extensively cultivated and naturalized in other regions of the world. Ryegrasses are naturally diploid, possessing a chromosome number of 2n = 14, and they share a close genetic relationship with fescues (Festuca). It is important to note that ryegrass should not be confused with rye, which is a distinct grain crop. The following species are recognized as distinct within the genus Lolium: Lolium canariense Steud. Scholz, Stierst., & Gaisberg Lolium multiflorum Lam. (commonly known as Italian ryegrass) Lolium perenne L. (commonly known as perennial ryegrass) Lolium persicum (commonly referred to as Persian ryegrass or Persian darnel) Lolium remotum Schrank Lolium rigidum Gaudin (also known as stiff darnel or Wimmera ryegrass) Lolium temulentum L. (commonly referred to as darnel or poison darnel) Ryegrasses include several species that are agriculturally significant, particularly for use in lawns, pastures, and as forage for livestock. These grasses are highly nutritious and serve as an important feed source for grazing and hay production. Additionally, ryegrasses are utilized in soil erosion control programs. In New Zealand, perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne) is the primary grazing grass, with approximately 10 million kilograms of certified seed produced annually. A wide variety of cultivars have been developed for different purposes. Perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne) is the most widely distributed and utilized species globally, serving both as a lawn grass and a forage crop. Like many cool-season grasses in the Poaceae family, ryegrass harbors a symbiotic fungal endophyte, either Epichloë or its close relative Neotyphodium, both of which belong to the fungal family Clavicipitaceae. However, some ryegrass species, particularly Lolium temulentum, are considered weeds that can significantly reduce the yield of wheat and other crops. Additionally, ryegrass pollen is a major allergen and a common cause of hay fever. Ryegrass is also used in the composition of grass tennis courts, including those at Wimbledon, where different blends of ryegrass are planted depending on the tournament requirements. The following are synonyms for various Lolium species: L. ambiguum = Lolium multiflorum L. annuum = Lolium temulentum L. arundinaceum = Festuca arundinacea L. berteronianum = Lolium temulentum L. brasilianum = Lolium perenne L. canadense = Lolium perenne L. crassiculme = Lolium rigidum L. cuneatum = Lolium temulentum L. dorei = Lolium persicum L. giganteum = Festuca gigantea L. gracile = Lolium temulentum L. lepturoides = Lolium rigidum subsp. lepturoides L. marschalli = Lolium perenne L. parabolicae = Lolium rigidum L. pratense = Festuca pratensis L. remotum = Lolium temulentum subsp. remotum L. romanum = Lolium multiflorum L. scabrum = Lolium multiflorum L. siculum = Lolium multiflorum L. subulatum = Lolium rigidum subsp. lepturoides L. teres = Lolium rigidum subsp. lepturoides
